payload.text: An online retailer tests whether a redesigned checkout page increases the proportion of visitors who complete a purchase. Of 400 arriving visitors, 200 are randomly assigned to see the current page (Layout A) and 200 to see the redesigned page (Layout B). Among Layout A visitors, 46 completed a purchase; among Layout B visitors, 66 completed a purchase.

stimuli.alt_text: A randomized experiment: 200 visitors see Layout A with 46 purchases; 200 see Layout B with 66 purchases.

payload.label: Purchases by layout (some cells left blank to complete)

stimuli.alt_text: Two-way table with completed-purchase counts 46 for Layout A and 66 for Layout B; the did-not-complete cells and column totals are blank.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain the purpose of randomly assigning visitors to the two layouts in this experiment.

criteria.description: Explains that random assignment tends to create two groups that are similar with respect to other variables, balancing potential confounding variables between the layouts.
Explains that this allows an observed difference in purchase rates to be attributed to the layout, supporting a cause-and-effect conclusion.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Complete the two-way table, then calculate the proportion of visitors who completed a purchase under each layout.

criteria.description: Completes the table correctly: Layout A did-not-complete = 154, Layout B did-not-complete = 134, completed total = 112, did-not-complete total = 288, grand total = 400.
Computes the Layout A purchase proportion 46/200 = 0.23.
Computes the Layout B purchase proportion 66/200 = 0.33.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe the association between layout and purchase completion shown by these data.

criteria.description: States the direction: Layout B had a higher purchase proportion than Layout A (0.33 versus 0.23), a difference of 0.10.
Interprets the association in context: in this experiment the redesigned page was associated with a greater proportion of completed purchases.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The retailer wants to know whether Layout B produces a higher purchase rate in general. Identify an appropriate inference procedure, state one condition and why it is met, and explain what kind of conclusion the experiment can and cannot support.

criteria.description: Identifies a two-sample (two-proportion) z-test for the difference between two proportions (a chi-square test of homogeneity is also acceptable).
States one appropriate condition and why it is met, for example Large Counts: each group's completed and not-completed counts (46, 154, 66, 134) are all at least 10.

Explains scope: because layout was randomly assigned, a significant difference would support a causal conclusion, but because visitors were not a random sample, generalizing beyond these visitors is limited.

accessibility.accommodation_notes: A partially completed two-way table is provided with alt_text; the table-completion response uses the table modality permitted by the frq-multifocus-2-3-4 archetype. Remaining responses are typed text and typed math.
